stimulus.text: Two engravings from Theodor de Bry's America series (1591), after drawings by Jacques Le Moyne de Morgues. The first shows Florida Indians planting seeds of beans and maize in cleared fields. The second shows the same people hunting deer disguised under deerskins. De Bry never visited North America; he engraved the scenes in Europe from watercolors painted by Jacques Le Moyne, a French artist with the Laudonnière expedition.
stimulus.source_note: Engravings from the shared image pool; Theodor de Bry (1591), after Jacques Le Moyne de Morgues, public domain (Library of Congress).

stem: The first engraving shows men and women planting seeds of beans and maize in cleared fields. Which conclusion about Native American societies before sustained European contact is best supported by this image?

options.text: All Native peoples in every region lived only by hunting and gathering.
options.misconception: Assumes every Native society lived the same way, by hunting alone.

options.text: Farming was an established, organized part of Native life in this region.
Europeans introduced maize and bean farming to North America in the 1500s.
options.misconception: Reverses the exchange: maize and beans were American crops Europeans found here.

options.text: Native peoples in this region planted crops only after Spanish missions arrived.
options.misconception: Puts Spanish missions before farming that already existed in the region.

rationales.A: The image shows people planting crops in prepared fields, so a claim that everyone lived only by hunting fails against the picture.
rationales.B: The engraving shows organized planting of maize and beans, which is direct evidence that farming was already established in this region before sustained contact.
rationales.C: Maize and beans were Native American crops grown long before Europeans arrived, so Europeans could not have introduced them.
rationales.D: The engraving shows Timucua farming as Le Moyne saw it in the 1560s, before the missions reached the region, so missions cannot explain the farming.
rationales.general:
1. Look at the hands. Men and women press seeds of beans and maize into cleared fields, working soil with tools.
2. Ask what the work means. Sowing seed in prepared ground is farming, and farming is a signature: it says people stayed put and fed themselves from this ground.
3. Ask what farming rules out. A people who plant are not just passing through or living off wild food.
4. Check the date. The engraving dates to 1591 and shows practices from before sustained contact.
Remember: when an image shows people working the land, ask what food system the work belongs to.
